p:
Because my concern— and have you all seen this within the DOC as well? I reviewed it— is what mechanism is there to track any phone calls between DOC employees and ICE? We saw some instances over email, and because that— there

was a written record, and that was why a written record was important, was, you know, DOI was able to identify these flagrant violations happening. But if there are phone calls that are happening, what mechanism does DOC have in place to ensure that there are not impermissible phone calls happening between between DOC employees and ICE agents. And, you know, obviously we're talking about an agency that does record phone calls between those who are incarcerated and otherwise. So what can we do here to ensure that there are not those impermissible phone calls happening?

I think, you know, we do have the ability to look at phone numbers. You know, we don't record employee phone calls. Uh, we do— would have the opportunity to look, and that might be part of what we perceive, as a good next step in the audit process when we engage with the city and the committee on this. But I– you know, again, I would say this: the answer to the issue that you're raising is primarily, and I think should be driven by training and robust training as to the limitation obligations with respect to the city laws

and our policy. That's where we had gaps initially, and, you know, I've really undertaken this mission to change that, you know, in a lot of ways. And again, to figure out how to get this training out robustly. So that's the first thing, is we need to have the staff in its entirety understand what the limitations and obligations are under the sanctuary city laws. Nonetheless, I do think we can do that, you know, a look into the phone numbers and otherwise, but you know, we're still talking about a very large agency. So, you know, we have to look and be very measured and targeted at how we look at that. I don't think it's necessarily an easy answer, but again, we are, are more than willing and will work with, you know, the Interagency Response Committee to figure out if that's a prudent measure to do or if we could expand on that.

I think that's gonna be an essential step, and there's no question that training is gonna be, you know, very important going forward. But on the other side of it is just the accountability measures in place too. You know, we can come back to this in more detail in a little

bit, but one of the instances here, as you well know, Deputy Commissioner, was an employee that had— was literally coordinating with ICE when the bus left Rikers Island, when it dropped off the individual on the other side on Hazen [sp?], and, you know, it— there's so much unmonitored communication that was happening in that instance, but those were serious legal violations of a regime we put in place. I do think it's gonna be critical that DOC also look at what to do, because it's in those everyday instances that these flagrant violations are happening. And understanding an agency this big, too, there has to be ways to ensure that employees, you know, if they get the training, that's important, but they may forget that training, or, you know, it may happen– they're not aware of it, or whatever it may be, in that moment there are these real-time instances happening that, you know, it's gonna be crucial that the agency look at much more carefully now than under the last administration.

And we agree with that. We do agree with that. But I would say, and, you know, I don't in any way intend to mitigate

the instance itself, you know, because it is a violation of the local laws. But, you know, what really happened there was what even DOI classified as an inadvertent cooperation. These communications in approved type of ways in a criminal investigation or intelligence gathering would have been fine. But what happened here is because of what was classified and rightly classified as a lack of training for those officers and guidance, there was not an awareness of what might have been happening. And that's what I think primarily we need to correct and what my intention is to correct with training. So that's a starting point. So you know, I do think that you're not wrong in identifying those areas where there are, but in this instance, I firmly believe, and I believe the OI believes, that if there was the appropriate training and guidance, that that might have been a trigger for that officer to more communicate with the, you know, General Counsel's office or someone else in the agency.

Right. And I would also just add that there's the known knowns, right, where there's inadvertent communication and training

can help, but there are also the known unknowns too, which is we're seeing now, as I highlighted before too, this federal government is resorting to any means possible to test in any way possible at any cost the boundaries of our sanctuary laws. In taking advantage of the fact that there are these criminal task forces and trying to slide in through the criminal way immigration issues, even if that— when they clearly fall outside of the criminal public safety exceptions in the laws. So that just raises the burden now of not just the inadvertent instances, but also a federal government that may deliberately– has shown deliberately, will do what they can to try to undermine and erode our laws.

I do want to represent one thing, to the council so that we do— we're talking about federal task forces and otherwise, and you know, I know that PD has— NYPD has a robust amount of those. Right now, actively, we only have three officers in our agency assigned to federal task forces. Two of them are assigned to the ATF or with the ATF, and one is assigned to the U.S. Marshals Office. So, we don't actively have any

officers with HSI or any other agencies. We are considering other ones such as the Postal Service and things like that. So, yeah, you're right that we have to make sure that the training and the information and the oversight is robust, but it's not necessarily a pervasive assignment throughout the island. It is very limited as it exists right now.
And what have been the conversations with DOC leadership about specialized training for those individuals who are part of those federal task forces? Because that's a big concern too.

Yeah, we went— we— I did that training myself. It was developed based off of a prior training that had been in existence, which I believe was built with MOI’s cooperation. I added to it, and I could represent to you that it is unequivocal as to what the obligations are. And I stress that, that even to the point that I say if you're uncertain as to what the interaction is or the question is, ask legal. If you're really certain about what the interaction is or the question is, ask legal. I really want the, you know, the onus

to be on me and my attorneys that work there to ensure that we're protecting everyone here, the individuals in custody as well as the officers and, you know, everyone else in the city to to make sure that that's, you know, adequate.

Another question, you know, shifting gears a bit, too. In December, the Department of Corrections had failed to testify at the request of the immigration hearing following the release of these DOI reports. Now, I understand now that we are in a different administration, and so I have two questions. One is, has the DOC attended to testify in person regarding immigration in the past six months, and will that policy change now going forward.
I'm sorry, could you repeat the question?
Sure.
I apologize.

In December, following the DOI– DOI report came out in September. In December, there was a hearing by the Immigration Committee. It's my understanding that the Immigration

Committee had requested DOI's presence to testify, and DOI did not show up. Has DOC attended any immigration hearing in the last six months and testified? And and what will be the department's position going forward should they be asked to testify at an immigration hearing?

Yeah, no, we did not appear then and we have not testified within the last six months, but I mean, to answer your question, we're present now. You know, so it is our intention to appear. You know, obviously that's in collaboration and communication with the mayor's office, but nonetheless we're present and ready to answer questions. And that would hold true for any Immigration Committee hearings as well?
I have no reason to believe otherwise.

Sure. Yeah, because I do think that will be an important way to have these conversations and ensure that the compliance is happening too on an ongoing basis as well. So at the February 15, 2023 oversight hearing on the New York City detainer laws, DOC testified

that ICE had never presented the department with the judicial warrant. Is that still the case? And if it's not the case, how many judicial warrants has DOC been presented with in the last year?

The— I believe that to still be the case. I have not, in my experience in working in this agency, seen a judicial warrant associated with a civil immigration detainer. I have seen— I'm sorry, we have had criminal arrest warrants, but they're distinct. That's not what's contemplated in the law. That's separate. And that was only two or three times. But, judicial warrants associated with a detainer, we've not seen.

So my question is then, how do we ensure compliance? Because part of those sanctuary laws requires, in the limited instances where one of the convictions that qualifies for, honoring a detainer request, it does require the presentation of a judicial warrant. And my understanding from legal services organizations otherwise is that sometimes ICE will be— will come to Rikers to take custody of someone because they have a qualifying conviction based on a request of

notification but without presenting a judicial warrant. Is that happening, one? And two, given the serious requirement in the law of a judicial warrant even for those qualifying convictions what will DOC do going forward to ensure that ICE is only presenting it— oh sorry, that DOC is honoring detainee requests when a judicial warrant is presented?

So the answer to your question is– well let me go back. The– yeah. It’s long-winded answer probably. Our longstanding policy does not rely on the first part of 9-131 regarding detaining someone and quote-unquote honoring a detainer, where we detain someone longer than their—
Correct, that’s right.
normal custody time.
Yes.

So what our policy is based on is the subdivision H of 9-131, which is a permits communication of a discharge date

when you have a detainer that doesn't have a— even if it doesn't have a judicial warrant, and there is either a qualifying conviction or the terrorist watch list, those qualifiers. That's the communication that happens in limited circumstances. And in that instance, that's where we do a review. It comes to the Legal Division. Does someone have this detainer request? Yes. Is it supported by an administrative warrant that establishes probable cause that the person is subject to removal proceedings? Yes. And then further assessments. Do they have a qualifying conviction? Is there any other qualifiers, or is there some other circumstance that we should not make the notification? So when I talked about in the testimony about the 18 transfers in 2024, the 25 in 2025, those were the circumstances. Our policies are clear, and our guidance from our attorneys and myself when we respond back to the ICE unit and or anyone who inquires of us, it's that the individual is not to be detained any longer than the normal discharge procedures. And that's our policy and that's our Legal Division mandate and guidance to that. So in

those circumstances, we are not conventionally honoring a detainer. Honoring a detainer means—
Correct, yes.
You know what it means.
Yes.
It's where we keep someone longer than we should.
Which is prohibited, yes.
And that's not what our policy dictates and our practices are.

Well, thank you for that clarification. That important. And yes, it's not about honoring a detainee request, but it's the communication information in those instances about discharge day. What is your understanding of the warrant requirement there? Is it– are you— is it an adminis— it is an administrative warrant or is it a judicial warrant? What is your understanding of the law as to when that communication about a discharge happens, and how do you ensure that that requirement is being met? That warrant requirement.

So under the communication, it is a detainer request, which is a formal form that's submitted to us, and it's also supplemented universally— I've never seen it without it— an administrative warrant that, that is signed by an immigration official that establishes the probable cause. That's in opposite of the judicial warrant. The judicial warrant would, in coordination with all the other qualifying convictions and otherwise, allow us to detain someone. So our practice is when we review the paperwork, if any of those aspects paperwork-wise is missing, we will not make a communication. We will deny or direct the ICE unit or anyone else to not make this communication or other.
Thank you. I'm trying to look for questions. I think Council Member Brewer has questions.

Thank you. You talked about training, and it's great that you're doing it. So do you do it for everybody? Do you hire outside, internal? And then of course, if people– you know, some situations may be after nine to five, so

who would people complain to, you know, if they had a situation? So just generally training.

So, training in general so far has been done primarily by myself or other members of the Legal Division. And so I have attorneys and I have two Deputy General Counsels. So we've both and all have presented again mostly at the promotional trainings. How we roll this out more widespread, we're actually– we're working with our Deputy Commissioner of Training now to– two things: to get into the recruit classes. So, that's most important because you get people fresh and coming into the Department so they don't have a misunderstanding from day one as to what our limitations are.
You have a class coming up?

There's one in now, and I'm actually trying to get— we're figuring out and coordinating when we could get in to speak to them about that. So there's 260-something, new recruits that are going through the academy. Subsequent to that, we'd also, again, we want to–

what the Deputy Commissioner of Training is building out is an in-service training course that we require on an annual basis officers come for— I forget exactly what the term is— maybe a three, four, five-day training, something along those lines. And we're going to work with him to ensure that we are part of that, and this is part of that, you know, somewhere within the block, to make sure that everyone's getting an annual refresher on what the laws are and updates, right? Because it could be updated and changed, and we want to make sure in addition to just issuing a teletype, which is important because that is intended to reach all members of the service, that it's also this in-person, you know– we give you the guidance and let you know even the nuances in terms of what you may encounter.
And if people use— if people see something, an infraction, but it's after hours, you said normally they would call you. So how would they do that if you're not there?

Well, we have a 24-hour legal line. We have an attorney of the day

who's on call. I'll just be candid, my phone is never off. So if it's something that has to come directly to me, I will answer it. In addition to that, we have a legal intake email address that is often used. And, you know, it's not that somebody will not be available. We do have the availability for that. And also our grievances, if that was another avenue to make a complaint. But I think we're more talking about a, you know, someone from the outside or a legal person, and we are available. We do have attorneys on call seven days a week.

And then, do you also— because the situation we heard earlier from Legal Services, obviously post- pre-administrative no transparency, etc. So it sounds to me like that's not going to happen again, but do you talk to legal services about these issues, or is that a no-no?

No, I've, I've had a number of conversations, you know, in special circumstances, or even allaying fears. You know, people think that we might be honoring something and we're not, and as it turns out, the people, you know, the individuals were released. So

I've been accessible, yeah, and again, we can, we can have these conversations. You know, I think we want to gauge the defenders on different things, you know, particularly as we've talked about, Council Member Brewer, the visits, you know, attorney visits. So I'm not opposed to having this be one of the conversations.
Okay. And then I should know this, but in social services we never ask people their immigration status. Is that also true in correction?
Yes, that is. We don't inquire about the legality or illegality of their presence here.

Okay. And then, how would— I guess what I'm trying to think of, how would any interaction, you know– I guess the way you're trying to prevent what has happened in the past is by training. Is that sort of what you're saying?
That's a start. That's the start.
Okay, are there any other places where you could be more transparent or that in addition to the training so that ICE doesn't have any input?

Well, I think that what DOI recommended and we started to do with at least whoever we're in a partnership with now is communicating with their leadership as to what our limitations and obligations are and making clear that we are only able to do whatever the enforcement is— criminal enforcement, intelligence gathering. So that's another avenue. So it's the training, communications with the partnerships, and then supervision, right? You know, so making sure that the supervisors are aware and that this obligation to notify the legal division or to notify particularized units is complied with. It's part of policy, and that there's multiple levels of oversight, not only from us on the legal side and the administrative side, but direct supervision of the officers themselves and in communication with agency partners.
And is the union leadership aware of what you're doing and also hopefully supportive?

I— we haven't spoken to them about it. I mean, you know, we do the trainings, and I could certainly communicate that if we think that's beneficial. But I've not been– I've, never encountered a union leader that would be opposed to more robust training for any of its members. So I think that's not— wouldn't be a concern, but I'll certainly convey that to the union leadership.
Thank you.

I'd like to note that the Deputy Speaker Natasha Williams is on Zoom. And now we'll turn it over to Council Member Aviles. Or is Council Member Avila not here? Okay. When she comes back, we'll turn it over to her. So I just want to go back to something, Deputy Commissioner, which I, you know– this was on my mind too, because we talked about administrative warrants, but I just checked on the administrative code, and in Section 9-131 requires that department may only honor a civil

immigration detainer by holding someone beyond the time or by notifying federal immigration authorities of such a person's release when the immigration authorities present the department with a judicial warrant for the detention of the person. So there is a judicial warrant requirement, and I'm not understanding why notification is happening without the presentation of a judicial warrant as opposed to administrative.

Yeah, the policy is based on Subdivision H of 9-131, which doesn't contemplate the honoring of the– So, it's persons not to be detained and talks about the communications. So what it says is shall not communicate about a discharge or, you know, there's other provisions. I'm sorry, I don't have the language memorized, but it's in that Subdivision H unless— and then it has the qualifying conviction and the person's appearance on entire watch list. So you have the presence of the detainer and we're not permitted to honor the detainer, right? That clear. We don't honor the detainer absent a judicial warrant and the qualifiers, but in the communication aspect

pursuant to Subdivision H, there is that, you know, ability to communicate about the discharge date, which is pri— I mean, not primarily, that's what these interactions are, and it requires, you know, the detainer essentially and does not require the judicial warrant for the communication, and then the qualifiers as far as the convictions and otherwise.

But what I'm having a hard time understanding is how does Section 8 operate? If you look at Section B1, right, it says— I'm going to read it again. The Department may only honor a civil immigration detainer by holding a person beyond the time when such person would be otherwise released from custody, which you all don't do, or by notifying federal immigration authorities of such person's release. So it's the notification of release in Section B1 that is only supposed to be happening with the judicial warrant. And I'm also wondering, how does Section— Subsection H override that?

I still do believe and think that– and again, this is longstanding policy that's been over two mayoral

administrations and through MOIA and also, you know, the City Law Department as its interpretation. My understanding and longstanding understanding is that that first subdivision really specifically applies to continued detention. So it's not just as about the notification as to the release date, it's the existence of the person's presence in custody, which— and also honoring it, meaning keeping the person in custody beyond their normal discharge time. The subdivision H is merely the notification of the discharge time without any honoring or continued detention pursuant to the detainer absent a judicial warrant. And I'm not trying to be coy. I mean, that's the—
[interposing] No, I– yes.
Yeah.

And I think if you all can provide some guidance to this committee too about that, because I'm also trying to understand. I understand it's been longstanding policy, but notification is written in the statute above, and it

seems that, you know, we're in the interpretation reading out that section.
Right. I'd be curious to see, and if you can provide this committee with the—
[interposing] We'll certainly have a follow-up where we outline that better. It's hard to do, you know, sitting here without paper and stuff.

Back and forth, right. Yep. We'll turn over to Council Member Avilés to have questions. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you so much, chairs. I'm sorry, give me one second. I had it open. I— apologies, since I've been in and out, you may have answered this question 17 times, so forgive me if that is in fact the case. But can you tell me the DOC ICE unit, how many people are in this unit, and what is exactly the unit does?

So it's– it's a subdivision of our– a subunit I'd say of our custody management unit. It's comprised of— it's very few people. I think it's three or four captains that

are active permanently and/or temporarily assigned there that assist with this. We need, you know– we need to stand up a unit in these circumstances to see and have a main point of contact for whenever there is an ICE detainer or there needs to be an inquiry for someone to call and see if any communication or if the ICE detainer is, you know, valid or in place or what the obligations are. So it's just merely a subunit, very small subunit of the custody management division that deals with these, reviews them, gives us the paperwork, communicates with the legal division as to, you know, again, the paperwork processes, qualifying convictions or otherwise. And then they will clear– “clear the warrant,” meaning to have the person discharged normally, or otherwise, you make this communication directly with immigration officials that we've been discussing. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Got it. Thank you. And in terms of– we understand NYPD has a much more extensive guidance. What is the guidance that DOC has provided in terms of how they're documenting requests that are coming in and that process?

Yeah. So, I, I mean, the guidance— we actually have what I'd consider pretty extensive guidance on this. I mean, it's a 19-page policy. There's multiple forms. The ICE unit has its own internal protocols where they do track, you know, this is where we get the information for our local reporting, the local law reporting, and also, you know, our own edification of what the process and numbers look like. So they have their own internal protocols, and then our policy is pretty robust when it comes to what the obligations are, where things are documented, and where they have to go. So I wouldn't say that it's more limited. I mean, by their very nature, the PD has a much broader scope of what they have to do while ours is narrow and focused. But I do think, again, a 19-page directive plus our teletypes which outline the obligations– and that's written guidance that's independent of whatever we do for, you know, again, what we're building out is training. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Great. Would you be able to provide that to the council for review?
I think it is in the D– COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: [interposing] It is?

We certainly will, but it's in the DOI report as attachments. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Great. Okay. In terms of– would the recommendations adopted by DOC have prevented DOC from sharing information about Mr. Villanueva?

I do think primarily the one main recommendation, as I mentioned to the Chair earlier, is the training aspect. I do believe in the nature of this interaction and the seeming misunderstanding or just lack of guidance that was given to the CIB officer that was involved, officers that were involved, I think stems from a, you know, primarily the absence of or lack or not adequate enough training, which we look to fix. So I think there's multiple layers here. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Yeah.

You know, the other recommendations go towards, you know, finding

out other incidents, but I think on these specific incidents, the training would have really made a difference. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Do you think the guidelines of the framework and guidelines of the law are too confusing? If we were to simplify the law to make it more straightforward, would that help in this regard?

I think quite candidly, to me they're not. I mean, it's nuanced and it could be difficult for the layperson to understand, and I do appreciate that. But we do make, and it's my job to make the training and the guidance internally unequivocal and clear. And I think we're able to do that within the boundaries of the law. So I really can't speak on how other people interpret. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: I appreciate that. But we've had these laws on the books for well over a decade, and there seems to be some level of confusion. So it seems like perhaps streamlining the law and making it clearer would help both our employees ensure that they can follow it, as well as the public to be able to articulate where the bounds

of the laws potentially fail. So, it feels like we should be looking at the policies and making sure if they seem to be confusing for anyone that we clarify that. Because we're going to train forever, and clearly we're seeing violations continuing to happen. So, something is wrong with the pie. In terms of the purpose– excuse me. We've seen this with NYPD. In terms of the recommendation around asking federal law enforcement to identify the purpose of the immigration request to ensure that it's legitimate law enforcement purpose, can you talk to us a little bit about that? That was a problem with NYPD as well. There were not real verifications because this engagement we see is based on relationship, you know, just a courtesy, law enforcement to law enforcement. So how are you training, and what is the guidance to make sure there is an actual real law enforcement immigration issue?

Sure, yeah. We— I mentioned earlier that we do have a very limited group of people that are actively engaged. I mean, right now it's three and it doesn't go much beyond, you know, several more whenever we have these

federal partnerships. So obviously the primary focus of that is to get to those individuals. Our personnel have a clear understanding as to what their limitations and obligations are, what our policy and the laws of the City of New York are. Additionally, we do, again, we've engaged now the leadership in those task forces from the federal agencies, which gives the guidance. And I've been, again, unequivocal with them as to what we cannot be doing, and they've been receptive to that. So we do have those two guardrails, but I also think there's, you know, again, any other types of things that we can do. The scripted— I think one of the recommendations here was like the scripted questions– becomes a little unwieldy, and obviously has been mentioned here, does that necessarily give us the answer? I want our officers to be able to appreciate and understand on their own without asking the questions as to, wait, what's happening here? And if there's a tinge of hesitance on their part, to communicate with their supervisors and leadership within the agency to make sure that this interaction, communication, and working arrangement is compliant with the local laws.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So, how do the officers— a small unit, obviously— how do they verify that what they are being told is in fact the case?

Yeah, they go through us. I'm sorry, Council Member, I apologize. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Can you walk me through? What does an officer do? Receives a call from DHS in Arizona, says, hey, I need this, whatever. What are the protocols that— what does the officer do then to verify that that is in fact the case and it is within the of the law? What are their next steps?

Yeah, so that scenario doesn't really happen in that way. The interactions that we've had here are where there was a working relationship in the task force, and there was an understanding, at least what the initial purpose of the task force was, this criminal enforcement. It was an operation that they actually named, and that was what DOI found to be the understanding of the correction officer. So in those circumstances, it's— if there's an understanding and something kind of lends outwards from that, that, you

know, seemingly is in furtherance of any immigration enforcement. Our instruction now, particularly since we've trained those individuals in the wake of the DOI report, is clear: contact the legal division. So that is— if there's any uncertainty or ambiguity in what the nature of the enforcement is, or it's— the scope seems to be outside of what the criminal or intelligence gathering purpose is, they have to make that communication. That's actually the process. Any other communication, I would say, is squarely limited and prohibited without the consent and advice of the ICE unit and the legal division. That's what our policy dictates. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So, in the context of NYPD, and maybe this is outside here, an officer calls another officer in a task force, they have a relationship. They claim a legitimate criminal activity, which would immediately— you'd assess that is within the bounds of the law, the officer takes it, because they have a relationship, They work together all the time. We found, in fact, there was no criminal basis. How— and there was no protocol for that officer to then verify that that

criminal basis that was told to them was, in fact, not legitimate. So I guess my question is, within the bounds of these relationships, right, where there's trust and colleagues, how do officers verify that the stuff that they are being told, the context for, for a detainer, is in fact true?
So you're asking— it's actually a really difficult question. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Yeah, no,
I don’t know that there's an answer all around. I mean, COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: We've seen it. We've seen it happen–

[interposing] Yeah. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So I was just curious, like, what kind of, what kind of protocols NYPD asserts it saw that instance and is trying— added an additional layer of guardrails there.

Right. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉ: So I guess in the same context, given the nature of these relationships, what are the additional guardrails do

you think would be apropos to ensure that officers are not getting caught in that scenario?
I mean, I hate to repeat myself in this– COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: [interposing] Yeah.

but I think it is the interaction with, with supervisors, the legal division, the– you know, the ICE unit, anyone else that has, you know, more knowledge and basis of knowledge of this. I mean, if you're asking me a scenario where they say, no, it's criminal, It's criminal, we're not doing anything else, and then we're just working with them, and then something happens on that end, it's a very difficult— I mean, that may be the time to explore the relationship, right? But I mean, these federal partnerships, we have to have a level— I mean, it's just— I'm just being honest, we have to have a level of professional trust and ethics in terms of your obligations to comply with the local laws and otherwise, because they are fruitful to us.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: I mean, if we had a federal government that actually was following the law, I could follow that rationale. But we are in a new context, in a new terrain where the law doesn't actually apply and they're not following it. So I would insert some skepticism and way to verify that what is actually what they're being told is in fact the case. I know that's difficult because there are relationships. However, we are in a very different situation, and I think I would urge the department to really consider if there is an additional layer of verification, both to protect honestly the staffers, who are— whose responsibility it is to follow the law of New York City, um, but also wanna protect their professional relationships. So I would just urge and encourage a little bit more interrogation and placement of guardrails there, because that is where we see the most serious infractions occurring, is in this interpersonal relationships of trust. And I think we certainly could explore that with the committee and the audit, you know, the audit that we're doing with the city partners. So, um, you—

we'll bring that to them and make that part of our assessment. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you. Thank you, Chairs.

Thank you, Council Member. Those are great questions. I wanted to go to some— another topic that Council Member Avilés covered too, but just to go through again. So when was the most recent training that DOC had done for staff, and what is the frequency now that we're doing?

So we've done– we did the trainings immediately subsequent to the DOI— well, becoming aware of the incidents. So that was about April and May. I actually sat down with the individuals involved right away, the– you know, them and the supervisors, and just went through the practices and policies. We developed the training and that was done. We've brought it to— I forget, I'm sorry, I'd have to get back to you as to the exact date of it, but when we get into the recruit classes, that's something that's been done. We've had an Assistant Commissioner assigned to oversee the

as a global matter. You know, again, this might be nuanced and specific to this.

ICE and Legal General Counsel.
Licensed General Counsel, okay.

You know, it was something that there was a misunderstanding of the nature of that. So in that circumstance, when there's a belief that the interaction was in furtherance of some type of criminal work or investigative work or intelligence building, that wouldn't require notification to us. What we're requiring and encouraging and stressing is that when it becomes unclear, or if there's any level of uncertainty as to what the nature of the

participation. So if and when that is explored and expanded, my intention— not my intention, my obligation and commitment will be to have similar communications at the outset with those supervisors in those units and agencies.

Thank you. And so, you know, I want to just revisit I think the importance of that discussion we're having before about the 9-131, because I did read quickly Subsection H2, and I'm not seeing— I think it would be helpful for DOC and Corp Counsel, the Law Department to provide, you know, their law on this too, their explanation. But the prior one, B, that we were talking about, talks about, you know, notification as well and does so in the context of a judicial warrant. requirement. Sure, totally.

Thank you, Chair Krishnan. Good afternoon. My name is Jason Taper, and I'm a legal fellow with the Surveillance Technology Oversight Project, or STOP. We advocate and litigate for New Yorkers' privacy rights, fighting discriminatory surveillance which is the subject I would like to focus on, but first I'd like to echo the rest of the ICE Out Coalition and call for this council to pass the TRUST Act, establish a universal right to counsel in immigration cases, and abolish the so-called gang database, because ICE uses

presence in a gang database as pretext for deportations. Regarding the previous administration, former Mayor Adams' complicity with ICE was both immoral and illegal. Though we are worried about the incomplete accounting provided by the Department of Corrections earlier, we are thankful that Mayor Mamdani has turned the page and is an ally in the fight against ICE. But unfortunately, the end of Adams' mayoralty was not the end of this problem. The infrastructure that Adams put in place is still here, and every day it still exists. The surveillance that we undergo risks giving ICE our private information. In order to truly be a sanctuary, we need to not just end collaboration with ICE itself, but also to end our city's complicity with the spyware companies that enable the horror that ICE inflicts. Let's name names. Our city public hospitals partner with Palantir. Palantir, as you may know, is an essential part of ICE's dragnet. Our tax dollars and our sensitive health data should not go to companies that support ICE. And no one should have to forego healthcare or any other essential service out of fear their data will end up with ICE. As another example,

Clearview AI is a facial recognition company with a $10 million contract with ICE and a contract with FDNY. Again, New York tax dollars supporting a key tool for ICE. It is exactly because ICE needs the collusion of local governments and spyware companies that New York City must end contract with Palantir, Clearview, and big surveillance more generally. And it's not enough simply to stop actively giving ICE’s spyware companies our tax dollars. We need to cut off the data pipeline. No more sharing data without a real warrant, cut— assigned by a judge. And importantly, we need to minimize the data we collect in the first place, because the only way to truly make sure ICE doesn't get their hands on our information is not to collect it in the first place. To conclude, we know that ICE's oppression is fueled by the collusion of local governments and spyware companies, but New York City can be a shining example that there are tangible, concrete ways that cities can fight for our immigrant neighbors. We can tear down the partnerships with big surveillance that fuel ICE, and we will not in fact rest until we abolish

ICE and power down our city's authoritarian surveillance. Thank you.

Good afternoon. Thank you to the Committee on Investigations and Oversight for holding this public hearing to address the urgent need to protect our immigrant communities in New York City. My name is Tania Matos. I'm the Executive Director of Unlocal, an immigration legal nonprofit providing immigration legal services. We are also part of the Pro Se Plus Project and the Rapid Response Legal Collaborative. I'm here to express my deep concern for our sanctuary laws and the breaches we have witnessed. Every day we work with individuals and families whose safety depends on whether the city truly holds up its sanctuary laws. We are living through a period of escalating detention and deportation. In this climate, New York City sanctuary laws are not just symbolic, they are life-saving. They prevent more New Yorkers from being funneled into detention where people face neglect, prolonged confinement, and in some cases even death. They also strengthen public safety by ensuring immigrant New Yorkers can interact with local government without

fear that their information will be shared with ICE. When that trust is undermined, the consequences are immediate. We have worked with individuals who are afraid to seek protection because they feared going to court, and court could expose them to immigration enforcement. We have advised parents who hesitated to access services for their U.S. citizen children out of fear it would put their family at risk. Even the perception that city agencies like NYPD and DOC are communicating with ICE and collaborating with Donald Trump and Stephen Miller's unconstitutional policies creates a ripple effect keeping people from reporting crimes, cooperating with investigations, or seeking emergency assistance, and even talking to their teachers within the Department of Education. This is why the passage of the New York City Trust Act is critical, and that is why continued support for the Pro Se Plus Project and Rapid Response Legal Collaborative is so vital. These protections ensure that safety and due process remain real for all New Yorkers. Thank you.

Good afternoon, and thank you to the City Council for having this hearing. My

name is Benjamin Remy, and I'm a Senior Coordinating Attorney at the New York Legal Assistance Group. I'm here today specifically to speak a little bit about what is happening inside of our immigration courthouses, which are just down the street from where we sit now. As some of you may be aware, I have been on the ground every single day at the immigration courthouses since ICE began detaining people at two of our immigration courts here in New York City, 26 Federal Plaza and 290 Broadway. My introduction to this phenomenon of ICE enforcement, which was unprecedented in our New York City immigration courts, was a mother who was brutally thrown to the ground right in front of me after her routine court hearing. Despite pleading with ICE agents that she had a child in school that she needed to be home for when her child returned home from school, she was thrown on the ground with a knee placed on her back as she continued to scream for her children. Little did I know that this was just a very small preview of the cruelty that I would see only increase and intensify over the following months. Months later, I was standing in front of another

courtroom surrounded by masked federal agents. As people began leaving the courtroom, the door opened and the first man to walk through naturally took a step back when he saw masked agents in front of him. The agents interpreted this as resisting and began screaming at him and tackled him to the floor, wrestled, and wrestled with him for several minutes while there were small children only feet behind him. I heard him begin screaming in agony and realized that he had been handcuffed so poorly that his wrist was bent at an extreme angle, and there was actually blood coming out of his wrist and onto the floor from the incorrect placement of the handcuffs. When I demanded that those federal agents fix those handcuffs, I was told that he wasn't even on their supposed list for immigration enforcement that day. Today, although the raw number of daily detentions in our courts have decreased, we still see the same level of brutality and cruelty when these detentions are made. We still see families split apart on a daily basis. And people who are doing their best to follow the rules and come to court with the document that they were instructed— that instructs them to be

in court that day are being punished for doing so. Just last week, I walked out with someone who had just finished with their routine hearing, and in the elevator, he confided in me that he had not slept at all the night before. He had just prayed and prayed the entire night that he would make it back home the next day. If there's anything that this evolution in ICE courthouse activity has taught me is that our work is far from done. ICE has demonstrated that they have no respect for our sanctuary laws here in New York City, and we must continue to work tirelessly to ensure that our institutions do not collude with the Department of Homeland Security. Finally, it is also imperative that City Council ensure that our immigrants have places to go for advice and support so that they can make informed decisions about how to best navigate today's treacherous landscape. This includes funding the work of legal service providers and community-based organizations who have proven their capacity to adapt to meet the needs of the immigrant community— of our immigrant community members and have built relationships of trust with

all of the diverse communities across our beautiful city. Thank you.

Thank you very much. I just have a couple follow-up questions. One is, we– as you all know, we've seen what happened at Canal Street, 26 Federal Plaza, as you testified to as well. How have these recent incidents and the work that you all have done, what have they shown to you about how they've impacted the willingness of the immigrant community to interact with law enforcement when they're the victim of a crime, to reach out to government when they need help or services in other ways? How has this had an effect on immigrant New Yorkers?

So I think the effect has been profound in a really horrific way. We've seen this climate of fear that has been cultivated by ICE enforcement, and it is now very deeply entrenched within the immigrant community. And I see folks every day when I go to court that are shaking when they enter the immigration court, that are oftentimes in tears before they even make it to their courtroom. They go online, they see the videos, they see

everything that's happening at these courthouses, and they're terrified to show up. And they became— they, they become placed in this impossible situation where they can either continue with their case and do the q “correct thing” and go about things the correct way, but they risk being detained, or they don't show up for court, they're ordered removed in absentia, and they lose any ability in the future to pursue their case. So it's an impossible situation for folks. And I have absolutely seen that extended to city institutions as well. Mothers that are nervous about getting prenatal care at hospitals because of lack of immigration status and a concern that the government will be— the city government will be sharing information with federal authorities. Kids that are afraid to go to school, people that are afraid to even go to a Social Security office to get their Social Security card, which they're entitled to when they have work authorization. So I see this on a daily basis of people being absolutely terrified, one, to show up to court, and two, to utilize any basic services that we have here in the city.

I'll just add that I've also seen that happen with individuals that have no immigration court hearing coming up, but they've lived here for 30 years, 40 years. They're afraid to go to the hospital. They're asking for accompaniment to go to the hospital because they're afraid or they heard in the news that immigration is outside of a hospital. It doesn't help that immigration is going into Columbia University, is standing outside of Department of Education schools that we've heard in Corona, Queens happen. We've had principals call me, and wave the flag that immigration is outside of their school, although not on the school premises, but, at that moment we have to advise them and tell them to kind of lock down, and make sure that they implement their safety protocol. But families are very nervous to do everyday things, and many— I know many also organizations that are trying to buy groceries for families, again, get the medication for individuals who are very afraid to step out their house.

Thank you. And my final question, um, and this may be more for— or any

of you on the panel, frankly. Is civil rights groups have raised concerns about the Fusion Center at Rikers. From a legal defense perspective, how does the real-time sharing of data through these centers undermine the judicial requirement that we've been talking about found in our detainee laws? If you can answer.
